title: HIPAA
summary: HIPAA is the United States federal law that governs the privacy and security of protected health information, and its security obligations are expressed through the Security Rule together with the Privacy Rule, the Breach Notification Rule and the Transactions and Code Sets Rule. The Security Rule is deliberately flexible and technology-neutral: it requires covered entities and their business associates to implement administrative, physical and technical safeguards that are reasonable and appropriate for their size, complexity and risk, and it sorts implementation specifications into required and addressable categories, where addressable means the organisation must either implement the specification or document why an equivalent alternative is reasonable and appropriate. The technical safeguards include access control, audit controls, integrity controls, person or entity authentication and transmission security, which in practice means unique user identification, role-based authorisation, emergency access procedures, automatic logoff, encryption in transit and at rest, and immutable audit logging of systems that touch electronic protected health information. Risk analysis is not optional and is the foundation of every other decision; a documented, current risk analysis tied to a remediation plan is the single artefact most often probed in an investigation. Business associate agreements extend obligations down the supply chain, and breach notification has a four-part risk assessment with defined timelines. Practitioners should treat ePHI data flow mapping as the prerequisite for meaningful segmentation and monitoring.
objectives: You will be able to separate the Privacy Rule, Security Rule, Breach Notification Rule and Transactions Rule obligations.
You will be able to classify an implementation specification as required or addressable and document the decision either way.
You will be able to perform and record a risk analysis that links threats, vulnerabilities and ePHI systems to remediation.
You will be able to implement technical safeguards including unique identification, emergency access and audit controls.
You will be able to run the four-factor breach risk assessment and determine notification obligations.
You will be able to manage business associate agreements and inherited responsibilities across a supply chain.

beginner.definition: HIPAA, short for the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, is a United States law that protects health information. That information covers records about treatment, diagnoses and payment for care. The law sets privacy and security rules for it. Clinics, hospitals, insurers and the companies serving them must follow those rules.
beginner.whyItMatters: Health records are valuable to criminals because they rarely change. A stolen name can be replaced, but a diagnosis cannot. The law expects you to study the risks to health data and to write down what you will fix. It also expects safeguards such as unique logins, audit logs and encryption. Missing those can bring heavy penalties.
howItWorks: Find every system that stores or moves health information about patients.
Study the risks to that information and write down what you find.
Apply safeguards such as unique logins, limited access and encryption in every place.
Keep audit records that show who opened which patient record and when.
Sign written agreements with any supplier that handles health data for you.
If data is exposed, assess the risk and notify people within the set time.
beginner.example: Picture a small clinic where every doctor uses the same shared login. It is convenient, but the audit trail cannot show who opened a patient file. If a celebrity's record leaks, the clinic cannot clear its staff or explain what happened. HIPAA expects each person to have their own account, so actions can be traced honestly.
takeaways: Know where health information lives, including inside your suppliers' systems.
Give every user a unique login so audit logs stay meaningful.
A written risk analysis is the foundation for every safeguard decision.
